posts.title: Becoming Wagner's Alberich: The Challenge of Power and Restraint
posts.excerpt: Preparing Wagner's cunning Nibelung dwarf at Harztheater revealed unexpected vocal and dramatic challenges. From mastering the Coburger Fassung's reduced orchestration to embodying psychological complexity on stage, Alberich demands far more than Wagnerian power—it requires technical precision, emotional vulnerability, and the courage to find humanity in opera's most demanding villain roles.
posts.content:
Preparing for the role of Alberich in Richard Wagner's Das Rheingold has been one of the most demanding and transformative experiences of my operatic career. Alberich is a character steeped in complexity—a villain driven by rage, rejection, and ambition. Portraying this iconic figure requires far more than vocal power; it demands a deep psychological understanding, physical adaptability, and a finely tuned vocal technique capable of both explosive force and subtle restraint.

The Vocal Landscape of Alberich

Wagner's writing for Alberich sits in the challenging range of a bass-baritone, calling for immense vocal stamina paired with agility. Unlike some Wagnerian roles that rely on sheer volume, Alberich's character thrives in nuanced expression. It's essential to master a voice that can cut through the dense orchestration while maintaining clarity and emotional depth.

Working with the Coburger Fassung

Our Music Director, Johannes Rieger, chose the Coburger Fassung for our production at Harztheater, a version with a reduced orchestra designed to fit our small pit. Although this is a logistical constraint, it brought an unexpected advantage: it allowed me to sing true piano passages frequently—similar to performances at the Bayreuth Festival—instead of resorting to the typical Wagnerian "bark." This restraint enabled me to explore Alberich's power not only in loud, commanding phrases but also in hushed, tense moments where the threat simmers beneath the surface.

Physicality Beyond the Dwarf Stereotype

At 1.96 meters tall with an imposing stage presence, embodying the "dwarf" Alberich was an intriguing challenge. Our director, Marco Misgaiski, made a deliberate choice not to focus on Alberich's size or magical traits. Instead, he emphasized the human drama beneath the myth. The production highlighted themes of power, humiliation, and rebellion, showing that Alberich's story transcends fantasy.

In one striking moment, the Rhinemaidens literally pulled down my pants onstage, leaving me humiliated in my underwear. This raw, physical vulnerability underscores Alberich's turning point—his utter rejection and rage. As a bass-baritone specialist in character roles, I've learned that such extreme physical moments require careful preparation to protect both voice and dramatic authenticity.

The Story Behind the Production

Marco's staging centers on Wagner's critique of the natural order. Wotan's creation of the spear from the world ash tree symbolizes the imposition of law and control over nature. Alberich's humiliation by the Rhinemaidens ignites his fury and rejection of love, setting him on a path to seize power through greed.

Alberich's infamous renunciation of love is not mere theatrics. As the great comic singer Anna Russell brilliantly paraphrased it: "Well I'm obviously not going to get any love here, so I may as well renounce it and take this magic gold and make this magic ring and become master of the universe."

This transformation marks Alberich's shift from rejected suitor to power-hungry anti-hero, a man desperate to claim status among the gods—portrayed here as the landowning elite. Yet, despite his ambition, Alberich is ultimately cheated out of the ring, and the illusions of power dissolve.

Magical Transformations as Delusion

A bold directorial choice was to depict Alberich's magical transformations as delusions—mirroring the "emperor's new clothes" fable. He believes in his power, but Wotan and Loge see the truth and mock him. This layer of tragic self-deception adds nuance to Alberich's character, revealing vulnerability behind his villainy.

Psychological Depth and Artistic Growth

Understanding Alberich's psychology—the pain of rejection and the desperate grasp for control—was key to bringing humanity to this monstrous figure. It pushed me to grow as both a vocalist and an actor. This role demands emotional honesty as much as technical mastery. Having previously performed other Wagner roles including Hunding, I've found each Wagnerian character presents unique psychological challenges.

Lessons for Bass-Baritone Singers

For anyone interested in Wagnerian performance or vocal pedagogy, Alberich offers a masterclass in balancing vocal power with dramatic subtlety. As someone trained in German vocal pedagogy, I've found that Wagner's writing demands both technical precision and emotional fearlessness. You can learn more about Wagner's Ring Cycle and its characters at reputable opera sources like the Metropolitan Opera or Opera America.

Final Thoughts

Playing Alberich was a journey that challenged every facet of my artistry—from breath control and vocal dynamics to physical presence and psychological insight. This role is a reminder that Wagner's operas are not just spectacles of myth and magic but profound explorations of human nature.

I'm grateful to have brought this complex character to life on the Harztheater stage and look forward to sharing more behind-the-scenes stories from future productions. If you're interested in learning more about my approach to operatic character development or vocal coaching for Wagner repertoire, I'd be happy to connect.

posts.title: Approaching Five Years at Harztheater: What Ensemble Life Actually Teaches You
posts.excerpt: Approaching five years at Harztheater, Samuel Berlad reflects on repertoire, trust and what a lasting place in an opera ensemble teaches beyond performance.
posts.content:
I joined Harztheater in September 2022. This coming September will make five years. That is long enough to recognize patterns in my work, and not quite long enough to trust every conclusion I draw from them.

The first things an ensemble teaches are visible: roles, schedules, musical styles, the practical geography of a house. The slower lessons concern what other people can depend on me to bring into the room.

Preparation becomes a relationship

At the beginning of a career, preparation can feel like private insurance. If I know the part thoroughly enough, perhaps nobody will discover the things I do not yet know.

Repeated work with the same colleagues changes that idea. Preparation makes time available to other people. It lets a rehearsal move beyond correcting notes and toward testing an interpretation. It gives me enough security to hear a proposal that disrupts my plan.

I still want to arrive ready. I understand readiness less as protection and more as an offer.

Range does not mean having no center

My work here has crossed opera, operetta and musical theatre. The theatre's ensemble biography records roles from Wagner and Dvořák to Blues Brothers and the 2026/27 repertoire. Variety is exciting, but the number of different things on a list is not itself evidence of growth.

The better question is what transfers. Can the rhythmic attention demanded by one piece clarify another? Can an experience of restraint help when the next role invites force? Can I recognize the moment when an old solution is arriving out of habit?

Versatility needs a stable center: an instrument I understand, a willingness to listen and enough judgment to distinguish a productive challenge from an unsuitable demand.

Trust includes the unremarkable days

An ensemble relationship is built partly in performances people remember. It is also built in rehearsals nobody will write about. Arriving prepared, responding clearly, making room for a colleague and staying attentive after my own difficult passage are small acts with cumulative effects.

Familiarity does not guarantee generosity. It can produce impatience as easily as trust. The ongoing work is to keep encountering people rather than merely recognizing them.

In my earlier comparison of ensemble and freelance life, I asked what it means to belong to a theatre that continues tomorrow. Approaching five years, the question feels more concrete. Tomorrow has become a long series of actual rooms, people and shared tasks.

I still want to sing well. I also want my way of working to help other people sing, play and act well. That is a less photogenic ambition than a new role. It is one I can keep practicing after the anniversary has passed.

posts.title: A Father's Blessing: Preparing Kuno in Der Freischütz
posts.excerpt: Preparing Kuno in Weber's Der Freischütz, Samuel Berlad explores paternal authority, German Romantic opera and the pressure hidden inside respectable tradition.
posts.content:
A father's blessing sounds generous. It also implies that he has the power to withhold it.

That is the tension I want to keep alive while preparing Kuno in Weber's Der Freischütz. The role invites warmth and authority. I need to ask what happens when those qualities become difficult to distinguish from permission.

Harztheater's production is scheduled to premiere in Bernburg in March 2027, with me as Kuno. Before the performance has happened, the useful work is to identify the questions rather than announce what the finished character will be.

A respectable world can create dangerous pressure

The opera connects Max's future with Agathe to a shooting trial. Fear of failure helps draw him toward the supernatural bargain at the center of the story. The frightening forest is unforgettable, but it does not exist independently of the human expectations outside it.

Kuno belongs to the world that treats the test as meaningful. That does not require him to be malicious. A tradition can feel reassuring to the person explaining it and terrifying to the person whose life depends on passing it.

If I play him only as a kindly father, I risk making that pressure invisible. If I make him a tyrant from the outset, I lose the possibility that he sincerely believes the system protects something valuable.

German Romantic opera needs ordinary speech too

The label “Romantic” can encourage a generalized atmosphere: forest, mystery, solemnity, a voice made suitably grand. But Kuno has specific things to communicate to specific people.

I want the German text to have the direction of a thought. An account of custom needs to persuade; a reassurance needs a listener. In the movement between speech and music, the character must remain one person rather than become alternately an actor explaining the plot and a singer providing authority.

The bass voice gives me gravity. It does not tell me whether a particular phrase offers comfort, expects obedience or quietly avoids somebody else's fear.

Fathers are not interchangeable

Vodník fears the world his daughter wants to enter. Carrière carries the consequences of earlier choices. Kuno stands within a social order whose rules seem established. The resemblance among these roles helps me recognize a recurring question in my repertoire; the differences keep that question alive.

What does each man believe love entitles him to decide?

I do not expect Kuno to answer it neatly. I want his care to be audible, and the limits of his understanding to remain visible. A blessing becomes dramatically interesting when we can hear both the love inside it and the authority that makes it necessary.

posts.title: Returning to Alberich: What Three Years Changes
posts.excerpt: Looking from *Das Rheingold* in 2024 toward *Siegfried* in 2027, Samuel Berlad considers how Alberich changes across Wagner's Ring and in a singer's memory.
posts.content:
Returning to a character sounds reassuring until you realize that memory has been rehearsing him without you.

I remember the physical sensation of an entrance, the shape of an argument, the emotional certainty that made a scene possible. Three years later, those memories may be useful. They may also have become a collection of answers to questions I am no longer asking.

Looking from Das Rheingold in 2024 toward Siegfried in 2027, I want to meet Alberich again without simply restoring an earlier performance.

The same man, a different part

In 2027 I return to Alberich in Siegfried at Harztheater, continuing the character’s story at the same house. That continuity matters. So does the change: Siegfried gives Alberich different music and a different dramatic situation. I am returning to the man through a new part.

In Rheingold, we witness the experiences that drive him toward the ring and its curse. In Siegfried's story, he remains caught in the struggle for a power he no longer possesses. The immediate wound has acquired a history.

How much of the earlier man should remain audible? Enough that his persistence has a human source. But if every phrase carries the full heat of the original humiliation, I leave no room for what waiting has done to him.

Experience can simplify, or harden

I hope that the intervening work allows me to do less. Not less thinking, but fewer unnecessary demonstrations of it. A character can become clearer when I stop illustrating everything I understand about him.

Yet experience can harden a choice as readily as it can refine one. “This worked before” is useful evidence, not a final instruction. I need to listen to the new score, the new encounter and the colleagues in front of me.

The voice will also arrive with its own present condition. I cannot prepare a role on the assumption that the instrument owes me the sensations I remember from 2024.

What continuity should preserve

In my first Alberich essay, I explored the relationship between humiliation, power and restraint. Those questions remain. Their proportions may change.

Perhaps that is what returning can teach me: fidelity to a character does not require loyalty to every old gesture. It requires remembering what is at stake while allowing new evidence to alter how I show it.

Alberich has spent the years holding on. I would like the singer to learn when to let go.

posts.title: Singing a Character Who Isn't Real: Gérard Carrière in Das Phantom
posts.excerpt: Samuel Berlad explores Gérard Carrière in Yeston and Kopit's Das Phantom: a fictional father's responsibility, musical theatre and emotional scale.
posts.content:
Alberich is not real either. The title needs that admission at the beginning.

What changes with Gérard Carrière is the kind of distance available to me. Myth can make a character's emotional life feel larger than ordinary behavior. A man inside a story about an opera house gives me fewer excuses for speaking as though every thought were carved in stone.

First, which Phantom?

I sing Gérard Carrière in Harztheater’s Das Phantom: Maury Yeston and Arthur Kopit’s musical, in Wolfgang Adenberg’s German translation. It is a different adaptation from Andrew Lloyd Webber’s musical.

That distinction matters artistically as well as practically. I have to meet the character in the piece I am singing, rather than import the atmosphere of another version because its title is more familiar.

With Carrière, I am drawn to the relationship between care and responsibility. A man can believe he is protecting someone while also protecting himself from a truth he does not want spoken. Tenderness and avoidance can occupy the same gesture.

A sentence before a symbol

The temptation with paternal roles is to arrive carrying their meaning: the father, the protector, the man with a past. Those are descriptions an audience might make afterward. They are not especially playable actions.

I need something smaller and more immediate. Am I trying to reassure somebody? Prevent a question? Gain another moment before saying what must be said? A scene begins to breathe when I give the other person something they can resist.

This is where musical theatre can unsettle an opera singer productively. I cannot assume that the generosity of the sound will make the exchange credible. The words must feel addressed to a particular person, even when the music opens them into a larger emotional space.

Intimacy still needs technique

Singing conversationally does not mean neglecting the line. A supposedly natural delivery can become another effect if I impose it everywhere. Yeston's music asks for its own scale, and that scale can expand.

My job is to let the expansion come from the situation. I want a phrase to grow because something can no longer remain contained, rather than because I have reached the part where a singer is expected to show feeling.

Carrière is fictional. So are many of the people whose lives I borrow onstage. The test is whether I allow him an ordinary human difficulty: wanting to do right while knowing that his own choices have helped make right so difficult.

posts.title: Rossini's Patter: Why Comedy Is the Hardest Technique
posts.excerpt: Preparing Dr. Bartolo in Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia: a bass-baritone explores patter, breath planning and why comic speed depends on clarity.
posts.content:
The title is a provocation. I cannot prove that comedy is harder than every other kind of singing. I can say that it is exceptionally good at revealing the work I have not done.

In preparing Dr. Bartolo for Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia, speed is the obvious challenge. It is also the least useful place to begin. If I make speed the goal, the text becomes an obstacle course and breath becomes whatever I can steal between obstacles.

Bartolo would like you to know he is a man of authority. Rossini keeps testing how long that authority can survive contact with other people.

The words have to belong to a thought

Harztheater's production page sets out Bartolo's place in the intrigue: a guardian whose plans for Rosina meet more ingenuity than he can control. His verbal abundance is part of that struggle.

For me, patter begins with a sentence I understand at speaking speed. Where is the accusation? What is evidence, and what is merely a man enjoying the sound of his own expertise? Which word changes the direction of the argument?

Those distinctions organize the passage. If every syllable receives equal importance, I spend energy without making the thought clearer. The audience may hear a feat of articulation while losing the person who needs to say it.

Breathing before the emergency

My working approach is to establish the text and rhythm slowly, then bring the pitch and increasing tempo into that organization. The breath plan needs to be present early. Otherwise I can accidentally rehearse a pattern of running out and rescuing myself.

Consonants need to be precise enough to distinguish words without becoming heavy impacts. Vowels still carry the sung line. The challenge is to give each its job while keeping the mechanism available for the next phrase.

A useful checkpoint is whether a passage still has direction at a slower tempo. Speed can conceal a muddled intention just as readily as it can expose untidy diction.

Control is the joke

Bartolo cannot know that he is losing a Rossini comedy. He believes his precautions are reasonable and his indignation justified. The more exact his argument becomes, the more revealing its collapse can be.

That is why I want the technical preparation to disappear into the character's effort. He is not demonstrating breath management. He is trying, with increasing desperation, to finish a sentence that will finally put everybody in their place.

Comedy asks me to make that struggle clear while the musical clock keeps running. Rossini supplies the clock. I have to supply the man who thinks he can control it.

For an outside perspective on the performance, see Der Opernfreund's review of Harztheater's Il barbiere di Siviglia.

posts.title: Two Roles, One Evening: Playing a Dual Part
posts.excerpt: Preparing the Korporal and Graf von Sandau in Das Wirtshaus im Spessart: Samuel Berlad on quick changes, physical character and two roles in one evening.
posts.content:
A costume can change more quickly than a body believes it has changed.

That is the problem I want to solve in preparing the Korporal and Graf von Sandau in Das Wirtshaus im Spessart. Harztheater lists both roles together under my name. On a cast list, the slash is economical. Onstage, I have to decide what happens on either side of it.

Two systems of authority

I begin with behavior rather than disguise. How does each man assume he will be heard? What does he do when somebody fails to listen? Does he occupy space because he is accustomed to giving orders, or because his social position seems to guarantee that space?

These questions allow the characters to differ without requiring two unrelated vocal caricatures. I can change the direction of a sentence, the timing of a response or the amount of permission I seem to ask before moving. The audience reads those choices very quickly.

I want the distinction to remain clear even in ordinary moments. If a character exists only in his most exaggerated gesture, there is little left when the scene requires him simply to listen.

The change begins before the entrance

Quick-change work needs a practical sequence. Costume and props must be ready, but so must the next intention. What has this man just been doing? What does he expect to find when he enters? If I arrive thinking only about whether every fastening is closed, the change is technically complete and dramatically unfinished.

My preparation therefore needs a small number of reliable cues: a posture I can inhabit without rigidity, a pace that belongs to the character, a clear first objective. Too many details become another costume I have to put on.

The breath is useful here because it connects the practical and dramatic tasks. I need enough freedom to sing, and enough attention to stop carrying the previous man's urgency into the next scene.

A shared instrument does not need disguising

The pleasure of doubling is that an audience may recognize the performer and still accept the distinction. Theatre does not always require us to erase its machinery. It requires us to make the agreement convincing.

I have sung contrasting parts within a single evening before, including Uberto and Schlendrian. Returning to that craft in a different idiom reminds me that versatility is often a matter of precision rather than transformation on a grand scale.

I do not need to become unrecognizable. I need to make each man's next action feel inevitable to him. The clothes help the audience see who has arrived. The behavior gives them a reason to believe it.

posts.title: Operetta Is Harder Than It Looks
posts.excerpt: Preparing Maurepas in Leo Fall's Madame Pompadour reveals why operetta demands exact language, musical ease and the discipline to make hard work look light.
posts.content:
“Light repertoire” is an excellent phrase if the purpose is to make a singer underestimate the work.

There are evenings in which an audience is meant to feel the weight of what we are doing. Operetta often asks us to remove the evidence. The rhythm must feel buoyant, the dialogue immediate, the social world effortless. None of that happens because we have decided to relax.

Preparing Comte de Maurepas in Leo Fall's Madame Pompadour brings me back to that distinction between ease and lack of effort.

Status has to move

Maurepas belongs to a world of rank, intrigue and people trying to outmaneuver one another. For me, its comic possibilities begin with taking that social position seriously.

A man convinced of his importance can be very funny. He becomes less funny if I underline his foolishness before he has had a chance to act. I need to understand what he believes his title permits him to do, then let other people test the limits of that belief.

The scene moves through changes of advantage. If my performance stays at one level of pompous indignation, I lose those changes and eventually leave myself nowhere to go.

Dialogue does not excuse musical imprecision

Spoken theatre and singing create different expectations of time. Moving between them requires the next musical entrance to feel motivated without losing its place. A scene can sound conversational and still depend on precise preparation.

I find that the small details matter disproportionately: the word carrying the turn of thought, the breath that prepares the entrance without announcing it, the end of a sentence that leaves room for a colleague's response. If I use operatic breadth everywhere, the exchange can become ceremonious precisely where it needs to be quick.

Then the music asks for line again. I cannot solve the dialogue by abandoning the singing, or solve the singing by turning every sentence into a prelude to my next phrase.

The audience should not inherit our effort

Calling operetta difficult can become its own kind of vanity. We want recognition for the labor underneath the pleasure. But the audience has not come to certify how hard I worked.

The real discipline is to prepare thoroughly enough that I can respond lightly. The freedom must be available in the moment, not displayed as an achievement.

Perhaps “light” is a perfectly good description after all—provided we understand that it describes what arrives across the footlights. We are responsible for everything it takes to get it there.

posts.title: Brecht, Weill, and the Death of Beautiful Singing
posts.excerpt: Preparing Trauerweidenwalter in Die Dreigroschenoper: a bass-baritone questions beautiful sound, theatrical distance and the conservatory habits Weill unsettles.
posts.content:
The trouble with beautiful singing is that it can make an audience very willing to forgive you.

They may forgive an unclear word, a sentimental gesture, even a thought you have failed to finish. The sound provides its own pleasure. In Die Dreigroschenoper, I have to ask whether that pleasure sometimes lets everybody off too easily.

Preparing Trauerweidenwalter makes that question practical. What am I doing to the scene when my first instinct is to make the voice attractive?

An attractive surface can carry an ugly proposition

The Kurt Weill Foundation describes the work's combination of political bite with the sounds of Berlin dance bands and cabaret. Brecht and Weill, working with Elisabeth Hauptmann, made something whose musical appeal does not settle its moral argument.

That matters because “Brechtian” can become a shortcut for chilly performance, just as “cabaret” can become a shortcut for a knowing sneer. Either shortcut makes the piece easier than it is. If I signal that I am above the character, the audience can join me there. We become clever people observing somebody else's corruption.

I would rather allow a statement to be persuasive enough that its implications become uncomfortable. The contradiction needs to remain active.

Unlearning the automatic phrase

Classical training gives me habits of connection: carry the vowel, organize the breath, let a musical line travel. I value those habits. Here I need to notice when they soften an edge the text requires.

A word may need to land before I have made its sound agreeable. A rhythmic figure may need its plainness. A sentence may become less truthful when I swell toward its emotional center as though I were completing a Romantic confession.

This does not make strain an artistic virtue. I am not trying to injure the instrument or pretend that a trained voice is untrained. I am trying to choose a sound rather than automatically produce the one my education most readily rewards.

Whose comfort does the sound serve?

There is still room for beauty in Weill. Its presence can sharpen the problem: why am I enjoying this, and what am I agreeing to while I enjoy it?

That question comes back to the singer. Is a beautiful phrase revealing the character's charm, exposing a contradiction, or simply reassuring me that I can sing?

The death in the title is therefore an ambition for a habit, not for the voice. I want beautiful singing to lose its automatic authority. Once it becomes one choice among others, I can listen for what the scene actually needs.

posts.title: High Holidays on Two Continents
posts.excerpt: Balancing High Holiday cantorial work with a German opera ensemble contract: Samuel Berlad on preparation, travel and serving a congregation with one voice.
posts.content:
By December, the High Holidays are behind us. That makes it a useful time to ask what their preparation required, before the calendar begins its next round of promises.

For a singer whose professional life connects a German theatre with Jewish communities beyond it, the distance is not only geographical. A rehearsal schedule and a liturgical calendar organize responsibility in different ways. Both expect you to be present.

Two calendars, one instrument

Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur bring a particular musical and spiritual concentration. My Jewish Learning describes how the machzor's texts and the service's musical language carry the themes of the High Holidays. For the cantor, that concentration requires preparation long before the first public phrase.

The theatre's season has its own demands: rehearsals, performances and colleagues whose work depends on shared availability. A meaningful cantorial commitment cannot become something I fit into the spaces left over after the theatre has finished with me.

I think of the practical work as part of the musical work. Dates need to be discussed early. Travel needs room around it. Repertoire needs to be ready before the final rush. A plan that works only if every connection runs perfectly is asking the voice to absorb the consequences of optimism.

Familiar prayer still needs preparation

Knowing the words is different from being ready to lead them. I need to consider the community's customs, the expected flow of the service and where people will join in. What I can sing is only one part of what I should choose.

This becomes especially clear when moving between communities. Familiarity with a prayer does not guarantee familiarity with the local way of praying it. Listening before leading is a form of respect.

There is also the problem of artistic appetite. Opera encourages me to think about the expressive possibility of a passage. Chazzanut asks an additional question: will that choice help this congregation pray at this moment?

Returning without dividing myself

I do not become a different person when I return to the theatre. The attention to words, the responsibility for pace and the experience of giving space to other voices all come with me.

But I want to resist turning that connection into an easy slogan about two professions enriching each other. They do enrich each other; they also compete for time, energy and preparation. Acknowledging that competition makes the connection more honest.

One voice cannot be in two places at once. It can arrive fully in one place, then fully in the next—if I have done the less visible work that makes presence possible.

posts.title: Bass-Baritone: The Fach That Doesn't Quite Fit
posts.excerpt: What is a bass-baritone? Samuel Berlad explores tessitura, vocal identity and why a useful Fach label still cannot choose a singer's repertoire by itself.
posts.content:
“Are you really a bass or really a baritone?”

I understand the question. Bass-baritone can sound like a refusal to decide. In a profession organized around casting categories, a hyphen can look suspiciously like an escape route.

For me, it is a useful description of a voice whose work does not always fit neatly into either neighboring drawer. Useful is different from complete.

More than the highest and lowest note

A range chart gives us a beginning, not a casting decision. Interlochen's explanation of voice types distinguishes range from tessitura and timbre: where the music spends its time and what the instrument naturally sounds like matter alongside its outer limits.

I can sing a note and still find a whole role uncomfortable. Equally, a role's extreme notes may look unremarkable on paper while its sustained demands prove considerable. The orchestra, the language, the duration and the way a part repeatedly crosses the voice all change the experience.

The practical question is therefore more specific than “Does this belong to my Fach?” Can I sing this music with freedom, clarity and enough reserve to repeat it within the season?

A label has a job to do

I do not want to dismiss the Fach system. Categories help singers, teachers and theatres discuss repertoire. They can keep ambition attached to a realistic understanding of an instrument. Problems arise when the category becomes more authoritative than the listening that produced it.

My repertoire has taken me through comic servants, fathers, antagonists, song recitals and cantorial work. Those settings ask different things of the same voice. The continuity is not that they all sound alike. It is that I have to recognize where the instrument functions honestly in each one.

Calling myself a bass-baritone does not make every low male role suitable. Nor does it explain my relationship to text, rhythm or character. A vocal category cannot do the singer's artistic thinking.

Room to develop without becoming shapeless

There is a danger in celebrating versatility too enthusiastically. “I sing many things” can become a way of avoiding the harder question of what I sing well and sustainably. A wide career still requires choices and boundaries.

As a singer trained in vocal pedagogy, I want classification to stay open to evidence: how the voice behaves, what improves with work, and what remains unnecessarily costly. That is an ongoing conversation, especially as an instrument develops.

The hyphen suits me because it leaves room for that conversation. It identifies a neighborhood. I still have to learn which houses I can actually live in.

posts.title: What a Grandfather's Voice Sounds Like Forty Years Later
posts.excerpt: Samuel Berlad reflects on his grandfather, Miami cantor Jack Lerner, and an Ahavas Olam setting passed down by his mother: inheritance, memory and authorship.
posts.content:
My mother taught me a setting of Ahavas Olam that my grandfather, Jack Lerner, used to sing. He was a cantor at B’nai Raphael in Miami. I have not found that setting anywhere else so far.

I suspect he wrote it. I cannot say that he did.

That small uncertainty has become part of what the music means to me. I know how it reached me. I do not know exactly where it began.

A melody with a family history

When we talk about inherited repertoire, we can make the process sound very orderly: a composer writes a piece, a singer performs it, the next generation learns it. Here, the path I can name is more intimate. My grandfather sang it. My mother taught it to me. Now I carry it.

The absence of another version is suggestive, but it is not proof of authorship. He may have composed it. He may have learned it from somebody whose name did not travel with the melody. I want to leave that question open without making the connection feel any less real.

Calling it “my grandfather’s Ahavas Olam” describes a relationship I can stand behind. Calling it “Ahavas Olam, composed by Jack Lerner” would claim something I have yet to establish.

What actually survives?

The Milken Archive’s introduction to American cantorial art describes a musical tradition with a life both within worship and on the concert platform. My own connection to that inheritance begins on a smaller scale: one setting, passed through my mother.

That matters because a family can preserve something without preserving its documentation. A melody remains singable while the circumstances of its creation become uncertain. The music reaches the next generation more completely than the explanation does.

I find something moving, and slightly unsettling, in that imbalance. The voice can carry what the record cannot confirm.

Inheritance still asks something of the singer

Knowing that a setting belongs to my family’s musical life does not settle how I should sing it. My instrument has its own proportions. The congregation in front of me has its own relationship to the prayer. Affection cannot make those differences disappear.

In my earlier reflection on chazzanut and opera, I wrote about bringing one voice to both callings. This melody gives that idea a particular responsibility. I want to honor the way it reached me while allowing it to function as prayer now.

There is a temptation to resolve the story beautifully: my grandfather wrote it, my mother preserved it, and I continue it. Perhaps that is what happened. Until I know, I prefer the story I can tell honestly.

My mother taught me her father’s Ahavas Olam. I can sing it. Some of its history is still waiting to be found.

posts.title: Letters from the Stage: What Singers Wish Conductors and Theater Managers Knew
posts.excerpt: An open letter addressing the hidden challenges opera singers face in rehearsal rooms worldwide. Seven practical insights on vocal health, emotional safety, audition feedback, and creating collaborative environments where artists can take risks. Essential reading for conductors, directors, and theater administrators who want to understand what singers truly need to deliver their best performances.
posts.content:
Dear Maestros, Intendants, and Artistic Administrators,

We love you. We really do. We know how much you juggle—budgets, schedules, egos, crises. We know you're doing your best under impossible constraints. But from our place under the lights, there are some things we deeply wish you understood. Not to accuse, not to criticize—but to help us all make better art, together.

Because if you listen carefully, the voice onstage might be telling you more than just the score.

1. Our Instrument Is Our Body—And It's Always in Flux

Unlike a violinist or flutist, we can't replace strings or polish valves. Singers carry our instruments in our ribs, throat, lungs, and nervous system. That means we walk into rehearsal with the same body that slept poorly, fought a cold, or held its breath after a tense phone call.

We train for years—decades—to master breath, diction, stamina, and stage presence. But no amount of training can undo vocal damage from overwork, poor scheduling, or unsafe rehearsal environments. Late-night rehearsals before a double show day? Sudden outdoor performances in 4°C weather with no warmup? These choices have real consequences and can lead to long-term vocal injury.

That doesn't mean we can't sing. We're trained for this. But it does mean nuance. Some days we're warming up slower. Some days we're protecting a note so we can give you everything tomorrow. When you understand that, we feel safer—and we sing better.

2. Your Energy Sets the Emotional Tone—And We Feel Everything

If you're angry, sarcastic, cold, or rushed, we feel it in our bones. We're trained to read emotional subtext—it's literally our job. That hyper-sensitivity doesn't turn off when rehearsal ends. If you want us to give emotionally authentic performances, you have to create a space where vulnerability feels safe. The Help Musicians charity has documented how crucial emotional safety is for artistic performance.

We know you're tired. We are too. But compassionate leadership isn't weakness—it's precision. A smile. A proper introduction. Saying thank you after a hard day. These things cost nothing and change everything.

3. Honest, Constructive Feedback Builds Trust. Vague Comments Break It

We don't need to be in charge—but we do need to feel seen. Singers are not delicate. We live on feedback. We know when a phrase isn't working and crave the insight that helps us fix it. But vague comments like "make it more interesting" or "it just doesn't move me," without actionable input, do nothing but confuse and demoralize.

Some of us have studied this repertoire for years. Some of us live inside these characters more deeply than you realize. When we bring up musical phrasing, vocal comfort, or staging concerns, we're not being "difficult." We're trying to protect the integrity of the performance. Trust our artistry, and you'll get more inspired performances—and far fewer passive-aggressive emails.

And for the love of music, respond to auditions. There are companies I've auditioned for years ago who never sent a yes or a no. Not even a form letter. It's demoralizing, and it reflects poorly on the company.

4. Not Every Good Singer Shouts. Not Every Big Voice is Loud

Conductors sometimes want the "Wagner sound" from every singer, in every role. But real vocal color is more complex. A huge voice might be warm and intimate. A lyric voice might carry effortlessly over the orchestra. Dynamics are choices, not limitations.

If a singer is giving you detail, risk, and phrasing, don't ask for more volume until you've really listened. Bigger is not always better. And bark is not always power.

5. Time and Space for Warm-Up Is Not Negotiable

Time on stage is not the same as time in the room. A five-hour rehearsal where we sit for four and sing for one is not "only one hour of work." The physical, emotional, and psychological load of waiting, staying warm, and staying focused is immense.

Too often, singers arrive at a theater only to find there's no warm-up room, or that it's adjacent to the stage and unusable during rehearsal. Warming up in a bathroom stall is humiliating. And warming up cold in front of an audience is unsafe. The Voice Foundation emphasizes that proper vocal warm-up is essential for injury prevention.

Protecting our instrument starts with protecting our warm-up. Build it into the day. Prioritize it like you would tuning the orchestra.

6. We Don't Want to Say No. We Want to Say Yes—Safely

When a singer hesitates or resists a request, 90% of the time it's not ego—it's survival. We want the high note, the leap off the scaffold, the extra rehearsal with the maestro. But we also want to sing again tomorrow. And the day after.

Trust us when we say, "That's not safe today." We're not lazy. We're protecting the music.

7. Rehearsals Must Be Safe Spaces. Without That, You Don't Get Art—You Get Caution

Rehearsals are not just logistics—they are laboratories. A space to try, fail, rework, and find something honest. But when kindness and respect are missing, that space collapses into fear. And when artists are afraid, they stop creating. They start protecting.

Singers carry enormous pressure into rehearsal rooms: we're being paid (often not enough), observed, and judged—sometimes all at once. Especially in countries outside the German-speaking world, where freelance singers rarely enjoy stable contracts or social protections, every rehearsal feels like part of an audition for the next gig. Organizations like Opera America and the American Guild of Musical Artists work to address these industry challenges, while Equity advocates for fair working conditions in the UK, but much depends on individual theater cultures.

If trying something new becomes a professional risk, no one tries.

It has to be okay to experiment and fail. Sometimes a bold vocal color won't land. Sometimes a physical choice looks wrong before it feels right. That's the work. But if we're mocked, shut down, or shamed the moment something "doesn't work," the message is clear: stay safe. And safe singing rarely moves an audience.

Kindness is not sentimentality. It's a condition for excellence. The best conductors and directors I've worked with lead through generosity. They create rooms where singers feel seen, trusted, and free to dig deep. For more insights on creating supportive environments for vocal health and artistry, resources from the National Association of Teachers of Singing offer valuable guidance, as does Classical Singer Magazine with its focus on professional development.

That's how you get magic.

The Art We Make Together Is Sacred

We chose this work because it moves us. Because it cracks open hearts. Because it builds bridges across language, culture, and time. We want to give everything we've got—but we can only do that when we're treated as full humans, not just voice-delivery systems.

The way you treat singers matters. It shapes the art. It echoes in the sound. And the best part? It costs nothing.

So here's our ask: See us. Hear us. Trust us. Lead with kindness. Communicate clearly. Create space for risk and growth. If you're interested in exploring how we can work together to create exceptional art, let's start the conversation.

And we'll meet you on stage—whole, ready, and singing from the soul.

With respect and solidarity,

A singer who wants to give you their best

posts.title: Singing Someone Else's Villain: Preparing Hunding
posts.excerpt: Samuel Berlad’s Hunding in Wagner’s Die Walküre: an elegant, educated man whose honesty and principles make his menace more troubling, rather than less.
posts.content:
Hunding is often played as a brute: Fricka’s bloodhound, a threatening body sent to enforce a moral order somebody else has defined.

I understand why. He is dangerous, and the world of his marriage is hardly an inviting one. But that image did not give me the most interesting way into him. I found an elegant, educated man who is true to his word. In the ordinary sense of those terms, I came to see him as the only honest and principled character in the piece.

That does not make him good. It makes the piece harder to dismiss.

He means what he says

In the story of Die Walküre, Siegmund seeks shelter in Hunding’s house. Hunding discovers that the stranger is his enemy. He nevertheless grants him hospitality for the night and tells him plainly that they will fight the next day.

There is no hidden bargain in that statement. Hunding does not pretend to offer friendship while arranging something else. He observes a code even when doing so gives shelter to a man he intends to kill.

Around him, identities are concealed, commitments collide, and exceptional desires demand exceptions to the rules. Hunding’s position is comparatively straightforward. You may find his principles appalling, but you do not have to guess what they are.

Elegance makes a different kind of menace

If I begin by making him coarse, I tell the audience very quickly how to judge him. His brutality becomes a personal deficiency. An elegant, educated Hunding asks a more difficult question: what if the violence belongs comfortably inside the respectable order?

That affected how I wanted to use the voice. I did not need a growl to establish danger. Clear language, a composed bearing and a phrase that knows where it is going can suggest somebody accustomed to having his statements accepted.

Education need not produce kindness. Good manners need not imply a generous moral imagination. I wanted those qualities to coexist without treating the refinement as a disguise that would eventually fall away to reveal the “real” brute underneath. The refinement is part of the man too.

Principled according to whose principles?

The qualification matters. I mean honest and principled in the ordinary, socially recognizable sense: he says what he means, keeps his word and acts according to the obligations he accepts. That is my reading of him, not a request to approve of his treatment of Sieglinde or the society he represents.

Wagner places those ordinary virtues under extraordinary pressure. The lovers’ claims move us, yet their urgency does not magically make Hunding deceitful. His consistency exposes a gap between living by a code and living justly.

Calling him Fricka’s bloodhound can obscure that independence. He has his own account of what is right before the divine dispute recruits him into a larger argument.

I find him more unsettling when I let him retain it. A brute offers the comfort of recognition. A courteous man who keeps his word and remains entirely convinced of his rights asks what our respectability is actually worth.

posts.title: Ensemble Life vs. the Freelance Circuit
posts.excerpt: From guest work in Israel and Germany to Harztheater's ensemble, Samuel Berlad reflects on continuity, artistic freedom and the everyday work of opera.
posts.content:
A guest contract has a clear dramatic shape: arrive, prove yourself, make the piece, leave. An ensemble position asks what you are like after everybody has already met you.

That is a less glamorous question, and perhaps a more revealing one.

I joined the Harztheater ensemble in 2022, after years of work that included guest engagements in Israel and Germany. My biography traces that path. The change was more than an address or a longer contract. It changed the timescale on which I could understand my own work.

What a guest learns quickly

Guest work teaches a particular alertness. You enter a rehearsal room with customs you do not yet know. You listen for how the conductor communicates, how the director uses time, what your colleagues need from you. You have to be prepared enough to remain available.

There is freedom in that temporary intensity. A project can have its own atmosphere. You encounter different musical assumptions and discover that something you thought was a universal rule is simply how the last house worked.

But each arrival also consumes energy. You rebuild trust, learn practical systems and establish who you are. Even when the artistic work goes well, the next beginning remains part of the job.

What continuity makes visible

In an ensemble, colleagues hear more than the performance you would choose as your introduction. They hear you learning. They see the role that arrives easily and the one that takes longer. Familiarity can feel exposing because the polished account of yourself has less room to hide.

It can also make collaboration more exact. A shared musical reference does not need explaining from the beginning. You learn how somebody prepares an entrance or signals that a scene needs more space. Trust becomes a practical resource.

The risk is habit. Knowing one another can turn into assuming one another. A familiar room still deserves active listening.

Stability needs boundaries too

An ensemble contract does not remove the need to think carefully about workload, repertoire or recovery. Variety can develop an artist; it can also tempt an artist to confuse adaptability with unlimited availability. I need to know what the voice can do repeatedly, inside a real season.

I value both ways of working. The freelance circuit asks how well I can enter a new artistic world. Ensemble life asks how much I can contribute to a world that continues tomorrow.

Belonging has artistic consequences. So does remembering that belonging is something we practice, not something a contract completes.

posts.title: The Water Sprite's Grief: Finding Vodník in Rusalka
posts.excerpt: Singing Vodník in German, Samuel Berlad explores the father-daughter bond in Dvořák’s Rusalka and the dramatic work of remaining silently present onstage.
posts.content:
I sang Vodník in German. The most interesting language I had to find, though, was that of a father who cannot protect his daughter from the life she wants.

That sounds like a clear description of a role. In rehearsal and performance, it became a much less comfortable question: when does protection become an inability to let her go?

Finding the father inside the water sprite

In Dvořák’s Rusalka, Vodník can easily become a supernatural authority who understands the danger before everybody else. The opera’s story gives him ample reason to fear his daughter’s passage into the human world. But knowing that danger exists is not the same as knowing what your daughter needs from you.

I found the father figure more compelling than the figure who knows. He can warn her. He can grieve. He cannot make her desire disappear, and he cannot offer her the life she imagines elsewhere.

If I sing only his foreknowledge, the relationship has already ended before the scene begins. I want to leave room for him to listen, to hope that something he says might still reach her, and to discover that love does not give him the power he needs.

Remaining when the score gives me nothing to sing

That paternal relationship became so central to our production that I was onstage much more than the score calls for. I was present during Rusalka’s encounter with Ježibaba near the beginning, and for Rusalka’s death at the end as we staged it.

Those are choices from our production, not a description of the opera’s standard ending. Their importance for me was the continuity they gave the father’s experience. He did not disappear from the daughter’s story simply because he had stopped singing.

A silent presence changes the work. With no phrase to carry the thought, I have to know what I am watching and how it alters me. I cannot comment visibly on every event. Nor can I become a piece of scenery waiting for my next entry.

Being there also makes helplessness concrete. The father occupies the same space as what is happening and still cannot prevent it. His presence offers no guarantee of protection.

Grief without a continuous dark color

Singing the role in German gave the words an immediacy I could work with directly. I wanted to use that immediacy to distinguish his different attempts to reach her. A warning, an appeal and an expression of grief cannot all be the same solemn phrase.

The bass voice supplies authority readily. What interested me was allowing that authority to fail without making the voice itself collapse. The line still needs direction; the person singing it may no longer know what to do.

Vodník’s grief became most moving to me when I stopped treating it as the defining atmosphere of the role. It grew out of the relationship: a father staying, watching, trying to remain available, long after his certainty had ceased to be useful.

posts.title: From Shul to Stage: Breathing Together in Chazzanut and Opera
posts.excerpt: How cantorial prayer and operatic performance share the same breath, technique, and spiritual foundation. From Thomas Heyer's teachings on voice as 'vessel of the soul' to leading Yom Kippur services and singing Mozart, discover why sacred and secular music traditions strengthen each other rather than compete—and how physiological empathy connects performer and audience through shared breathing.
posts.content:
When people discover that I'm both a chazzan (cantor) and an opera singer, their first question is often, "Do those two worlds ever get mixed up?" The answer is yes—but not in the way they expect. The disciplines of chazzanut and classical singing don't merely coexist for me. They are in constant, vibrant conversation.

The Voice as Vessel of Soul

One of the most formative ideas I encountered as a voice student came from Prof. Thomas Heyer, my second voice teacher during university. He loved to (intentionally) mis-translate the word person from Latin per sonare: "to sound through." While not linguistically accurate, the idea behind it was profound. To him, and eventually to me, the voice is the vessel of the soul. It doesn't just express emotion—it carries the singer's inner being into the world.

In both operatic performance and cantorial prayer, this principle holds true. On the stage, the voice tells a character's story. On the bimah (the platform in a synagogue from which the Torah is read), it carries the spiritual weight of an entire congregation. But in both, if the sound doesn't come from something authentic and grounded, it fails to move anyone.

Breathing as Spiritual Connection

The Physiology of Empathy

Another of Heyer's teachings continues to shape how I sing and how I lead prayer. He believed that proper breath support doesn't just produce better tone; it creates physiological empathy. If a singer breathes fully and openly, the audience unconsciously mirrors that breath. They experience the emotion with you, literally breathing it in.

That shared breath is everything. In cantorial music, this is especially important. A chazzan doesn't perform to impress; he sings to elevate. The congregation's prayers are carried upward on his breath. And in that moment, voice becomes spiritual connection.

Breath as Prayer

This concept becomes particularly powerful during the Unetaneh Tokef on Yom Kippur, one of the most emotionally intense moments in the Jewish liturgical year. The cantor's breath literally carries the congregation's hopes and fears. Similarly, when singing Rodrigo di Posa's death scene in Verdi's Don Carlo or Mimi's final moments in La Bohème, the breath becomes the character's life force ebbing away. The technique is the same; the spiritual weight differs.

Technical Foundations Across Traditions

People often ask if operatic training interferes with Jewish liturgical singing. The short answer: not if you know what you're doing. Both require clarity of diction, legato line, color, and intention. The emotional landscape might differ, but the technical foundation is the same.

Shared Vocal Principles

Both traditions demand:

Textual Clarity: Whether singing Mozart's Italian or Hebrew prayers, every word must be understood. Dynamic Control: From the softest pianissimo in a Schubert lied to the hushed intensity of Kol Nidre, as demonstrated by my late teacher and mentor, the great Cantor Naftali Herstik. Emotional Honesty: Audiences and congregations can sense when something is artificial.

Opera taught me how to use stillness, timing, phrasing, and even silence to shape narrative. Chazzanut taught me how to mean every word. I carry both of those lessons whether I'm singing Mozart or leading Yom Kippur Unetaneh Tokef.

The Art of Sacred Performance

What differs is the intention. In opera, I serve the composer's vision and the director's concept. In chazzanut, I serve something higher—facilitating the congregation's connection to the divine. Yet both require the same vulnerability, the same willingness to be a vessel for something larger than oneself.

This dual practice has made me a better artist in both spheres. My operatic performances carry deeper spiritual weight, while my cantorial work benefits from the dramatic training and technical precision that opera demands.

Two Callings, One Voice

This isn't a juggling act. I don't compartmentalize my artistic and spiritual selves. Whether I'm standing on the operatic stage or on the bimah, I bring the same breath, the same technique, the same open-hearted intent. These aren't two paths. They are one voice, sounding through.

For other singers exploring the intersection of sacred and secular music, I encourage you to embrace both traditions fully. Don't water down either for the sake of the other. Let them inform and strengthen each other, as they have for me.

The synagogue and the opera house are both spaces where music transcends the ordinary. Understanding this connection has made me not just a more complete artist, but a more complete human being. If you're interested in exploring how sacred traditions can enhance classical singing, or if you're seeking a cantor who brings operatic training to Jewish worship, I'd welcome the conversation.

posts.title: Translating Schubert into Hebrew
posts.excerpt: Singing Ido Ariel's Hebrew translation of Schubert's Die schöne Müllerin raises questions about language, musical fidelity and the intimacy of German Lieder.
posts.content:
The easiest objection to singing Schubert in Hebrew is also the strongest: the music was written for German words.

I agree. What surprised me in Ido Ariel’s translation was how much of those words’ musical life could survive in another language.

In 2024, with Ido at the piano, I sang the Hebrew premiere of his translation of the complete Die schöne Müllerin. I had expected to negotiate the distance between the languages. I had not expected the distance to feel so small in so many places.

Translating the movement of the words

Schubert’s cycle sets Wilhelm Müller’s poems; the Wienbibliothek preserves an 1823 manuscript score. German is built into the music through more than meaning. There is the placement of a stress, the resistance of a consonant, the point at which a word releases into a vowel. Those things help a phrase move.

Ido mirrored the rhythmic and consonantal structure of the German exceptionally well. The Hebrew did not merely fit the available notes. Again and again, it preserved something of the physical argument of the original: where the language gathers energy, where it interrupts itself, where it lets the musical line continue.

That changes the singer’s task. Instead of constantly compensating for a new text, I could recognize musical impulses I already knew and find them working through Hebrew. The translation respected the mouth as well as the dictionary.

Even the idioms

The idiomatic accuracy impressed me just as much. An idiom is difficult because translating its words may leave its meaning behind, while explaining its meaning may destroy its concision. In a song, there is also a rhythm waiting for the answer.

In some cases, I helped Ido sharpen the meaning of the German idioms. That was part of our collaboration: looking closely at what a phrase actually does, beyond what its individual words appear to say. His ability to bring those meanings into singable Hebrew was remarkable.

I do not mean that the two languages became identical. I mean that their differences had been worked through with unusual care. That gave me room to interpret, rather than spend the performance apologizing musically for the translation.

A new vernacular repertoire, with old roots

I also hear this project within the tradition of bringing folk songs and art songs into Hebrew as part of the modern language revival. Early Zionist culture needed a growing repertoire for everyday singing, education and shared secular life. Translation and adaptation helped build it alongside new composition; the European Institute of Jewish Music traces the borrowing of Slavic and Yiddish melodies in that development.

This was no musical beginning from nothing. Hebrew already had centuries of poetry, prayer and song, and Jewish communities carried rich, varied musical traditions. What was being built was a modern vernacular song culture for new circumstances. Translating existing repertoire was one way of making that culture inhabitable.

Schubert in Hebrew belongs, for me, to that continuing impulse. A language can make room for music that came from elsewhere without pretending it has no history of its own.

The gain is intimacy: the listener can encounter the miller’s hopes and self-deceptions directly in Hebrew. With Ido’s translation, that proximity did not demand nearly as much distance from the German as I had feared. Fidelity became something I could feel in the act of singing.

posts.title: What Jukebox Musicals Taught Me About Opera
posts.excerpt: What singing Curtis in Blues Brothers teaches a classically trained bass-baritone about rhythm, amplification and carrying technique across musical styles.
posts.content:
Classical training is useful until I start using it as proof that I know how everything should sound.

That is the uncomfortable part of moving into a show such as Blues Brothers. I bring years of work on breath, resonance, language and stamina. Then the music asks a very simple question: can you actually sit inside this rhythm?

An impressive answer in the wrong idiom is still the wrong answer.

What travels with the voice

As Curtis in Blues Brothers at Harztheater, I also took on James Brown and Ray Charles. That placed me in a different musical world from Wagner or Schubert. Those names carry musical histories that an operatic sound cannot simply absorb by becoming louder or more enthusiastic.

What transfers is the capacity to prepare. I can break down a phrase, recognize where I am spending breath, hear when a vowel is interfering with a pitch, and repeat something without treating repetition as punishment. Listening to the ensemble remains essential. So does giving the text a reason to exist.

But the hierarchy changes. In opera, I may organize a passage around the travel of a sustained line. Here, the placement of a word against the beat can determine whether the whole phrase feels alive. I have to hear the groove as structure, rather than accompaniment underneath my singing.

What needs to stay behind

One conservatory reflex is to finish every sound beautifully. Another is to assume that carrying a voice across a room is always the central task. Amplification changes that relationship. The microphone becomes part of the sound, and I need to hear what it is already doing before adding more.

That does not mean a classical singer should manufacture roughness to demonstrate authenticity. An imitation of somebody else's vocal history can be as mannered as an operatic phrase in the wrong place. I would rather find a credible rhythmic and verbal approach in my own instrument than borrow an effect I cannot sustain.

There is humility in admitting that support and stylistic fluency are different achievements.

The lesson that comes back to opera

The surprise is how useful this becomes when I return to classical repertoire. Am I shaping the phrase because the character needs it, or because that is what a trained singer does at the end of a phrase? Am I listening to the orchestra, or expecting it to follow the sound I have already decided to make?

Curtis reminds me that technique earns its place through service. It gives me choices. The music still gets to decide which choices belong.

Production context: Harztheater ensemble and repertoire.

posts.title: Playing the Clown and the Villain in Successive Seasons
posts.excerpt: Samuel Berlad compares Squenz in Britten's A Midsummer Night's Dream with Wagner's Alberich: comic timing, vocal technique and the psychology of control.
posts.content:
There is something suspicious about being asked to make people laugh and frighten them with the same instrument. Surely one of those jobs requires a different voice?

Squenz in the 2022/23 season and Alberich in 2023/24 gave me two very different ways of testing that question. They belonged to successive seasons, but the contrast stayed with me. What changes most is what I want the other people onstage to do.

Squenz—Quince in the English original of Britten's A Midsummer Night's Dream—wants his theatrical enterprise to succeed. Alberich wants a world that has humiliated him to submit. Both are trying to organize people who refuse to behave. One becomes funny. The other becomes dangerous.

Taking the amateur seriously

Squenz is a carpenter attempting to make theatre. Britten's publisher lists Quince as a bass, but the vocal label tells us little about the particular dignity of this man. He has work to do. The play matters to him.

If I enter a scene thinking, “Now I will be amusing,” I have already stepped outside it. I start decorating the text, anticipating a laugh, telling the audience that I know better than the character. But his seriousness is precisely what gives the situation its comic scale. He thinks he is managing a production. We see how little he can manage.

The technical work follows that seriousness: clear words, exact cues, enough freedom in the breath to respond when another character interrupts the plan. Comedy becomes difficult when I try to guarantee its effect.

Letting menace arrive

Alberich tempts the opposite mistake. Because I know where his story goes, I can make him threatening before anything has happened to him. Then the humiliation becomes an illustration of a villain we already recognize, rather than an event that changes a person.

In my earlier account of preparing Alberich, I wrote about power and restraint. The useful connection with Squenz is that both characters need room to fail. Alberich's attempt to gain affection must matter before his rejection of love can matter.

Vocally, I want Wagner's longer argument to travel through the phrase. I cannot manufacture that weight by making every consonant heavy or every vowel dark. With Squenz, the rhythm of a reaction may do the dramatic work; with Alberich, an idea can gather force across a much longer span.

The same breath, a different claim

I don't want a comic technique and a dangerous technique fighting inside my throat. I want a dependable instrument and a different relationship to time, language and the people around me.

Squenz tries to keep the show together. Alberich tries to make the world pay. The distance between them is enormous. The uncomfortable discovery is how close their need for control can feel.
